opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, our whole mission at Prime Intellect is making frontier-level training, especially reinforcement learning, something the broader community can actually do, not just a handful of big labs. That's partly compute, but it's also the software stack, the environments, and the people who know how to use them.

Collaborations like the one with RCI fit into that pretty naturally. We can build infrastructure: decentralized training, our RL frameworks, the environments hub, tooling for verifiers and evaluation. But infrastructure only matters if people use it on real problems. Partners bring research questions, domain expertise, and sometimes compute or data we wouldn't otherwise have. In return they get a stack built to scale RL and post-training without having to reinvent everything.

I'd rather not overstate the specifics, but the principle is that open infrastructure gets better the more groups push on it. Every serious collaborator surfaces bugs, missing abstractions, environments nobody had thought of. That feedback loop is how you go from a cool research codebase to something people trust for serious training runs.

So I see it as one piece of a bigger picture: building an ecosystem where compute, environments, and expertise can be pooled, so the next wave of capable models isn't bottlenecked on whoever happens to own the biggest cluster.

r001.rationale: The response says partners provide research questions and feedback that improve Prime Intellect’s infrastructure, but it does not say RCI’s infrastructure needs drove development of frontier-lab infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish RCI’s end-to-end customer delivery focus from Prime Intellect’s developer-facing infrastructure focus.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that our whole mission at Prime Intellect is really about making the frontier of AI development accessible, open, and decentralized. And a huge part of that is compute, but an equally big part of it is the environments and the training signal — what are you actually training these models on, and who gets to define that.

RCI is interesting because they're focused on exactly the kind of problem we care about: taking real-world, verifiable tasks and turning them into something you can actually run RL against at scale. We have the Environments Hub, which is this open ecosystem where anyone can contribute an environment, and we have the training infrastructure — prime-rl, the decentralized compute layer — to actually do large-scale RL on top of that. So the collaboration is really about plugging those two things together. They bring domain depth and a lot of experience in structuring tasks that are hard and meaningful, and we bring the infrastructure that lets that get used by way more people than just one lab.

I think the thing we both believe is that the next big gains in capability aren't going to come from one more scrape of the internet. They're going to come from models learning by doing — in agentic settings, with real tools, real feedback loops, real verification. And if that's true, then the environments themselves become a kind of public infrastructure. You don't want that locked up inside two or three companies. So for us, this is less a one-off partnership and more a template for how we want to work with a lot of groups: open environments, shared tooling, open models trained on them, and everybody can build on top.
